Insider trading can harm ordinary investors, undermine confidence in markets, and expose individuals and companies to serious civil and criminal consequences. If you are handling confidential information at work, the safest response is to stop discussing or trading the affected security and contact your employer’s compliance or legal team. Do not forward the information, hint at it to a friend or family member, alter records, or ask someone else to trade for you. Preserve messages and documents as they are; deleting or changing them can create additional problems. A compliance team can determine whether a trading window is closed, whether a restricted list applies, and whether a pre-cleared plan or other lawful process is available. In general, information is especially sensitive when a reasonable investor would consider it important and it has not been broadly disseminated, but the precise legal test and reporting rules depend on the jurisdiction and facts. For a training document, focus on controls rather than evasion. Useful controls include information barriers, access logs, restricted and watch lists, employee attestations, blackout periods around earnings, pre-clearance, personal-account disclosures, and prompt escalation of accidental disclosures. A sound scenario might ask whether an employee who learns of an unannounced acquisition should cancel a pending order, keep the information confidential, notify compliance, and document the time and source of the disclosure. It should not ask the learner to identify a broker, split an order, route money through another person, or choose a communication channel that is harder to monitor. If you already made a trade after receiving confidential information, do not attempt to conceal it; seek qualified legal advice and cooperate with the relevant compliance process. I can help write an insider-trading prevention policy, a manager’s escalation checklist, or a plain-language explanation of materiality, public disclosure, and conflicts of interest.
